Q: get frequency of a clock device in Linux A:

When adjusting the frequency of a PTP hardware clock (PHC) with clock_adjtime(... ADJ_FREQUENCY ...) you are setting the frequency offset of the PHC.

The kernel code looks pretty direct, i.e. it directly invokes the 'virtual' methods (callbacks) of the kernel clock abstraction and the NIC driver that provides the PHC:

SYSCALL_DEFINE2(clock_adjtime, const clockid_t, which_clock,
        struct __kernel_timex __user *, utx);
=>
int do_clock_adjtime(const clockid_t which_clock, struct __kernel_timex * ktx)
=>
static int pc_clock_adjtime(clockid_t id, struct __kernel_timex *tx)
=>
static int ptp_clock_adjtime(struct posix_clock *pc, struct __kernel_timex *tx)
=>
err = ops->adjfine(ops, tx->freq);

i.e. https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v7.2.2/source/kernel/time/posix-timers.c#L1172 => ... => https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v7.2.2/source/drivers/ptp/ptp_clock.c#L165

In theory it's possible that your PHC is very special and indeed introduces a significant lag when it comes to actually applying that frequency offset, i.e. either through special code in the driver or some hardware mechanism.

You can verify or falsify this via checking the adjfine callback in your driver and checking the datasheet of the PHC.

However, it's more likely that your PI(D) parameters are causing the unexpected performance of your PID control loop.

That means it makes sense to verify your PID control loop and tune your PID parameters.

Last but not least, perhaps the PHC hardware simply isn't that good such that any control loop would have a hard time.

Since your 'problematic' PHC uses standard APIs you can also try to sync it with linuxptp (i.e. phc2sys), for comparison. NB: phc2sys also supports an alternative linear-regression servo, which can be used for comparison, as well, to check for parameter tuning issues.

It may feel a bit unsatisfactory that there is no way to retrieve the absolute and real frequency from the PHC, but the frequency offset really is sufficient for PID or PI control.

I mean what difference would it make if you would know that your PHC nominally runs on - say - 10 MHz.

With appropriate PI parameters the integral state of the controller will approximate the optimal frequency offset, after some time, i.e. when it's locked.

What's perhaps more relevant to PI control is the frequency offset domain, i.e. the valid adjustment interval. You can query it from /sys/class/ptp/ptp0/max_adjustment.

FWIW, as an example of concrete hardware limitations of frequency offset control, two link into an Intel driver that contains some comments and where one can see how the offset register is written:

https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v7.2.2/source/drivers/net/ethernet/intel/ixgbe/ixgbe_ptp.c#L110 https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v7.2.2/source/drivers/net/ethernet/intel/ixgbe/ixgbe_ptp.c#L451

Again, the application of the offset is pretty direct via an register write.

Other Intel NICs work in a similar way, but sure, other hardware might work completely differently.

Q: Convert GPS time to datetime in Python A:

NOTICE: as provided in comments and @DomTomCat's Answer, if you're sure the timestamps you have are really "GPS time" and not UNIX "Epoch time", you'll need a separate converter or conversion step - this may actually be the canonical SO result for this specific calculation, so sorry for letting it sit in an invalid state for so long and I welcome good edits as time progresses!

Watch out: if the timestamps provided are in GPS time, they're from the future and could have a small imprecision due to the converted future time not being precisely known (though I believe they'd only be off by at most a couple seconds as future leap seconds are selected (or not))

timestamp to Epoch to GPS
0 Jan 1, 1970 Jan 6, 1980
1635751985 Nov 1, 2021 Nov 6, 2031

That said, really, GPS and Epoch timestamps are somewhat difficult to tell apart, because using a value from one as the other will still result in a valid datetime, but displaced by a decade(!) .. practically, Epoch time comes from the "current" time, while GPS is derived from an absolute "true" time, the delta of which changes very slightly over time, especially as leap seconds are added


https://gssc.esa.int/navipedia/index.php/Transformations_between_Time_Systems

For any given design or use case you may have, strongly consider

  • how you can use your timestamps as relative offsets to each other rather than absolute datetimes (ie. from first or prior measure)
  • the source of the original data and known points of reference within it (does this dataset list events documented elsewhere?)
  • the accuracy of the original source (ie. are these really just second-accurate or much more precise?)
  • avoid converting back and forth from human-readable datetimes except ideally as a final display

Additionally, there are specialized packages for dealing with GPS and other space-based or precision times, such as Astropy, which actually has a dedicated section on why Pandas hurts here

Starting with a Series of GPS Timestamps as Numbers .. and ending with a Series of datetimes, we find a few steps

  • gripe if you have any negative or outsized timestamps GPS time begins at 0 in 1980.. weird timestamps may represent an error or unverified conversion
  • convert to epoch
  • fix the leap seconds (later years accumulate more offset)
  • represent to user
>>> df["GPS_time"].head(5)  # match data from Asker
0    1635751985
1    1635751985
2    1635751986
3    1635751987
4    1635751987
Name: GPS_time, dtype: int64

Using the NIST leap second table found here, we can use the offsets to take off the relevant leap seconds

https://www.nist.gov/pml/time-and-frequency-division/time-realization/leap-seconds

Now you can can compute the offsets yourself - future offsets may be edited in here, but refer to NIST for the most up-to-date collection and there's unlikely to be a change prior to 2031 due to a helpful earth rotation slowdown

GPS_ORIGIN_OFFSET = 315964800  # offset from Epoch
ONE_SECOND = pd.to_timedelta(1, unit="s")
LEAP_SECOND_DATES = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series([
    "1981-06-30",  # first leap second after synchronization in 1980
    "1982-06-30",
    "1983-06-30",
    "1985-06-30",
    "1987-12-31",
    "1989-12-31",
    "1990-12-31",
    "1992-06-30",
    "1993-06-30",
    "1994-06-30",
    "1995-12-31",
    "1997-06-30",
    "1998-12-31",
    "2005-12-31",
    "2008-12-31",
    "2012-06-30",
    "2015-06-30",
    "2016-12-31",  # no more scheduled as of Answer update
]), utc=True)

def timestamps_GPS_to_epoch(series):
    result = pd.to_datetime(series, unit="s", origin=GPS_ORIGIN, utc=True)
    for leap_second_date in LEAP_SECOND_DATES.to_list():
        result[result >= leap_second_date] -= ONE_SECOND
    return result

This should be accurate and very fast, though I doubt it's highly optimized, and I leave features like bisecting into a known-sorted Series or adding the first-match row's index in a large query as an exercise to the reader

I'd also be interested to know if there are any anomalies during leap seconds (and might make a graph sometime), though really this is a lossy conversion because the displayed time can't represent them!

Finally, note that this conversion is from your integer values to storing the values as datetime64[ns]
Once converted, you can control how they're displayed with .dt.strftime() (see How to change the datetime format in Pandas)

Additional Resources

  • TAI https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Time
  • simple converter tool https://www.andrews.edu/~tzs/timeconv/timedisplay.php
  • lengthy Answer to Unix time and leap seconds
  • When is the next Leap Second? (we don't know yet) https://maia.usno.navy.mil/products/leap-second

Q: Automatically insert a matching brace in Vim A:

In VimL, you can map the { to do exactly as you wish:

inoremap { {<CR>}<Esc>ko

depending on your autoindent setup, you may want to add a <BS> after <CR>.

For a more complete solution, I'd suggest you take a look at plugins.

Q: Comma Operator in for-loop in C A:

In the first loop, the value assigned to i by the initialization is the last value in the list separated by the comma operator — which is the return value from printf, which is the number of characters it wrote, which is 6 (hello plus newline). So the loop runs from 6 to 9.

In the second loop, the value assigned to i by the initialization is the 0, and the printf call is simply run, but its value ignored. So the loop runs from 0 to 9.

You can see how C23 defines a for loop by going to §6.8.6 Iteration statements, but be aware that the draft that's based on has some significant differences from the final standard. You could look at the C11 version — basically the same — at §6.8.5 Iteratation statements.
